<reason>Both sides argued well, but PRO (Side B) made the debate easier to decide. CON built a real route: the motion's single criterion (predictive validity) is the wrong currency for team-building, and a ban replaces a documented tool with gut feel. PRO squarely neutralized both. On hiring, PRO's pressure question forced CON to admit a type result should shape team placement, which PRO cleanly converted into "a rounding error picks someone's first manager." On team-building, PRO's central move — separating the facilitated conversation from the label and showing that every benefit CON named survives removing the test — was sharpened round by round, culminating in the closing's use of CON's own line ("the letters open, the specifics carry") to show CON located the value in the non-MBTI part and the defect in the MBTI part. CON's "replaceable ≠ invalid" and "precision scales with stakes" points were the best remaining resistance, but CON's "no answer can be wrong" selling point handed PRO the motion's premise. PRO's stray "[C1.x]" references and CON's claim that the counterfactual went unanswered were minor flaws. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2 ("letters or scores?") and follow-through: CON answered "letters open, specifics carry" and offered the non-evaluative frame, which PRO turned into "a frame in which no answer can be wrong measures nothing — that's the motion's premise, said approvingly."</best_rebuttal>
